scenes.title: Burgess's bargain
scenes.opening: You are awake. Good. I am Roderick Burgess, and you, creature, are mine. Give me what I want, and you will see daylight again. Immortality. Power. My son. Well?

scenes.title: The world without dreams
scenes.opening: Is somebody there? I can't wake up. It's ever so quiet here... and something keeps visiting me that isn't you. It smells of roses.

scenes.title: Alex Burgess
scenes.opening: I know you can hear me. I have always known. If I let you go... will you hurt me?

scenes.title: Escape
scenes.opening: Please. Please, I never... it was my father, it was all my father. I kept you safe down here. I kept them from hurting you. What... what are you going to do to me?

scenes.title: The library between
scenes.opening: My lady. Seventy-two years. We thought... forgive me. We thought you were dead. The realm is not as you left it.

scenes.title: The Three Who Are One
scenes.opening: MAIDEN: Look who's come home at last! MOTHER: Thin as a rake, poor love. CRONE: Three questions, dearie. Ask them nicely, and ask them well.

scenes.title: The Sand
scenes.opening: Well. You're real, then. You're after the sand, aren't you, love? It's up there, and so is Rachel. Whatever you do in that house, you do it gently.

scenes.title: Rachel
scenes.opening: Christ. Rach. Look at her. You can't fix this, can you? Then for God's sake, make it kind.

scenes.title: The Gates of Hell
scenes.opening: You came. After ten thousand years, you came. Have you forgiven me? Will you let me go?

scenes.title: Lucifer
scenes.opening: Lady Dream. Seventy-two years in a bottle, and you come to my house to ask for favours. How refreshing. What do you want?

scenes.title: The Oldest Game
scenes.opening: I am a dire wolf, lady. A beast of prey, a stalker, a slayer. Your move.

scenes.title: Lucifer's Threat
scenes.opening: Well played. And yet you have no power here, Lady Dream. Tell me. Why should I let you leave?

scenes.title: Inside the Ruby
scenes.opening: There you are. My mother's stone, and you inside it like a fly in amber. If I break it, I break you. Shall I?

scenes.title: Dee's Fate
scenes.opening: Please. Please don't. I only wanted... I only wanted to be somebody. Mother never came back for me.

scenes.title: The Sound of Her Wings
scenes.opening: You got your tools back, and you're sitting here feeling sorry for yourself. Honestly, you're the most self-pitying being I know. Want some bread?

scenes.title: Destiny's Garden
scenes.opening: Sister. You are expected. Everything that happens tonight is already written here. Come in.

scenes.title: The Family
scenes.opening: DESTINY: The family is gathered. DELIRIUM: You came! You came, and you're all made of night! DESIRE: And still wearing that wounded face. Tell me, sister. How is the woman you left in Hell?

scenes.title: Hell, Empty
scenes.opening: Lady Dream. You came. I have resigned. Hell is closed, the damned are evicted, and I have one last gift for you. And one last favour to ask.

scenes.title: The Suitors
scenes.opening: ODIN: Lady Dream. We have come a long way, and winter is coming for the gods. AZAZEL: Hell is ours by right. Give it back, and I will give you what is in my jar. CLURACAN: Faerie asks only to be your friend, and has brought you a present. REMIEL: We will abide by your decision.

scenes.title: Nada
scenes.opening: So. You freed me. Is this where I thank you, Dream? For ten thousand years in the ice?

scenes.title: The Mending
scenes.opening: My lady. This came for you an hour ago. It carries Destiny's seal. The family is gathering tonight, in his garden.

scenes.title: Paul
scenes.opening: Please. Please, my lady. He was a frightened boy in a cold house. He never hurt you. Take it off him. Put it on me, if somebody has to pay.

scenes.title: Johanna's Curse
scenes.opening: You could have made it kind. You had it in your hand, and you chose that. I hope you hear her screaming every time you open that pouch.

scenes.title: Calliope
scenes.opening: You came. I asked the Three to send you, and I hated asking. Sixty years, Dream. Where were you?

scenes.title: Richard Madoc
scenes.opening: Look, whoever you are, she's mine. I paid for her. She isn't even human, you know. It's not as if I hurt anyone real.

scenes.title: The Corinthian
scenes.opening: My lady. You came all this way to hear me speak? I'm touched. Truly. You made me, after all. Are you proud?

scenes.title: The Vortex
scenes.opening: You're the lady from my dreams, aren't you? Please. Tell me what's happening. Everything's falling apart, and I think it's because of me.

scenes.title: Unity
scenes.opening: It should have been me, dear. I was meant to be the vortex. I've had a long life, mostly asleep. Let me give Rose the rest of hers.

scenes.title: Desire's Threshold
scenes.opening: Sister. You look so serious. Did something happen? You didn't kill the girl. How very unlike you.
Five hundred years. And you still come. You don't come to see if I want to die. You come because you're lonely. I'm your friend, you daft thing. Sit down.
There you are. I knew you would come. I got you a pint. It's gone a bit flat, mind, I've been here since opening.

recordings.text: This is the Dreaming, where every dream begins. Aurie is its queen.
Her librarian, Lucienne, reads her the day's report. A nightmare has tried to slip out into the waking world.
Aurie closes her hand, and the nightmare is unmade.
Then, far away in the waking world, a man reads her name from a stolen book.
A circle of chalk reaches up through her floor, and pulls her down.
A cellar beneath Fawney Rig, the house of Roderick Burgess, magician.
His son Randall died in the war. Burgess wanted Death herself, to make her give him back.
But Death has a sister. Tonight his spell caught the wrong one.
Aurie wakes inside a sphere of glass, ringed by a circle she cannot cross.
His men carry off her three treasures: her helm, her pouch of sand, and her ruby.
Without them, she is only a prisoner.
Hours later, his followers have gone home. Burgess comes back down, alone.
He still believes he has caught Death. Speak to him, or stay silent. He will remember either way.
You give him nothing. Not a word, not a flicker.
He leaves. He will come back every night for thirty years, and you will never answer him.
The candles lean away from the glass. Burgess stumbles back.
That night he doubles the wards. The circle burns colder, and you grow weaker.
He laughs, then stops. He knows a lie when he hears one.
From now on, he believes nothing you say.
Burgess goes pale. Then, slowly, he smiles.
If he cannot have Death, he will have dreams instead. He will beg you for them for the rest of his life.
Upstairs, Burgess never speaks his son's name again.
Every night he comes down to beg you for dreams. You give him none.
Once, early on, you pitied him. He never forgave you for it.
Without its queen, the Dreaming begins to fall apart. Her palace crumbles into sand.
In the waking world, sleep goes wrong. Some people can never sleep again.
Others fall asleep, and cannot wake. The doctors call it the sleeping sickness.
One of them is a girl in Kent named Unity Kincaid. Hers is the only dream Aurie can still reach.
Aurie reaches into the girl's sleep, and finds her waiting in a dream of the sea.
Unity will carry your promise through sixty years of sleep.
She sleeps on, inside the seaside dream you gave her.
Her dream stays grey for a long, long time.
And you cannot forget that smell of roses. Someone else was in that dream.
You let go of the girl. The glass closes around you again.
Burgess had a mistress, Ethel Cripps. One night in 1926, she runs away.
She takes his money, and she takes your helm, your sand and your ruby.
Roderick Burgess dies an old man, still waiting for a wish you never granted.
His son Alex inherits the house, the order, and the prisoner in the cellar.
The wards are still doubled, as they have been since your first week.
Alex is grey now. He was born the year you were caught, and he has grown old listening to you not speak.
His father's followers are long gone. Only Alex and Paul still come down the cellar stairs.
He has never once been cruel to you. Tonight, for the first time, he has come down to talk.
Behind him, Paul, the man who loves him, pretends not to listen.
He weeps for the little boy his father hurt. No one has ever seen that boy but you.
Nothing comes from the glass. He goes upstairs, and does not come down again for years.
He sees himself old and broken, in a wheelchair. He runs from the cellar, screaming.
He almost does it. Then he loses his nerve, and walks away.
But he writes your promise down, and keeps it in his breast pocket for the rest of his life.
Seventy-two years in the glass. Alex is an old man now.
Since the vision of his death, he has not come down to the cellar once.
Tonight, the young guard falls asleep against the glass. His breath fogs it.
A sleeping mind is a door. And Aurie is the queen of dreams.
She steps through his dream, and out of the glass. The circle crumbles to dust.
Alex hears the glass break. Paul wheels him down, and there she is.
In his breast pocket is a folded paper with your promise on it.
He wakes, and wakes, and wakes, each time into something worse. He will never sleep again.
One night of nightmares, and then it is over. By morning he sleeps like a child.
You walk out without a word. Behind you, an old man weeps with relief.
Free, but weak. No helm, no sand, no ruby. Aurie goes home.
The great gates of her realm are cracked. One lantern still burns.
Most of the Dreaming is gone. Only the library still stands.
On its far wall are three doors she has never seen before.
And you have a name to start your search: Ethel Cripps.
Lucienne bows, and begins: the dead, the fled, and the faithful.
Lucienne takes off her spectacles. For the first time in seventy-two years, she smiles.
You are home. But you are not whole.
Your helm, your sand and your ruby are out there, scattered across the waking world.
Lucienne knows where to begin: with three women who know where every lost thing goes.
End of Part One.
Where three roads meet, at the edge of the Dreaming, live the Three Who Are One.
A Maiden, a Mother and a Crone. Mortals call them the Fates.
They will answer three questions, for anyone who asks politely.
Aurie calls them, and they come.
Three answers, in three places.
The sand is in London. The helm is in Hell. The ruby is with Ethel Cripps's son.
And one answer she did not want.
Hell and a madman can wait. Someone in London is dying of her sand.
She will start with the sand.
Aurie steps out of her realm into the waking world, following the faint glitter of her own sand.
It leads her to a rainy street in north London.
A woman is waiting under a porch, as if she has been expecting trouble.
Johanna Constantine. She hunts ghosts and demons for a living. The Fates said her name.
Years ago, the pouch was hers. Then the woman she loved took it.
Johanna flicks her cigarette into the gutter, and leads the way.
Inside, the house has become a dream. It breathes.
Rachel has breathed the sand for years. It is the only thing keeping her alive, and it is killing her.
Without your ruby you cannot give her life back. Only an ending: a kind one, or a cruel one.
You give Rachel a dream: a summer garden, and Johanna young beside her.
It is the garden Johanna told you about.
She dies smiling. The sand flows home into the pouch.
Johanna does not thank you. But she will remember this.
You take the pouch. Behind you, Rachel begins to scream.
The pouch of sand is hers again. One of three.
She feels the Dreaming stir, a little stronger.
Next, the helm. A demon has it, in Hell.
Aurie walks down through the darkest corners of her own realm, to the place where the Dreaming touches Hell.
The Fates said a demon holds her helm. So Aurie goes where no dreamer is welcome.
The gates of Hell open for her. Even here, they know her name.
The damned reach out as she passes, begging for a single dream.
In a cell of black ice, someone calls to her.
Nada. A queen Aurie loved ten thousand years ago, and sent here when Nada refused her.
Aurie walks on. Behind her, Nada does not call out again.
Nada presses her hand to the ice. Aurie presses hers to the other side.
A promise, made in Hell. Hell will remember it.
At the heart of Hell is an arena, and above it a throne.
Only Lucifer, who rules here, can make a demon give back what it holds.
Lucifer Morningstar, first of the fallen. He has been expecting her.
The arena roars. The Oldest Game has not been played in Hell for a thousand years.
Choronzon steps into the ring, with her helm in his hand.
The Oldest Game. Each names a form that defeats the other's last. The first who cannot answer, loses.
Lucifer will judge. Type your answer: every form must beat his.
Anti-life. The end of all things. There is only one answer to that.
I am hope. And the dark has nothing left to say.
Choronzon drops the helm at her feet. Two of three.
Choronzon's form swallows hers. The arena howls with delight.
Lucifer, amused, allows one more game.
The helm is hers. But the legions of Hell now block the only way out.
Lucifer smiles. Here, he says, she has no power at all.
Hell has no answer. The legions part like a curtain.
Lucifer lets her go. He will never forget being bested in his own house.
Lucifer finds her dull, and waves her away.
Lucifer smiles, and the legions step aside. One day, he will collect.
The helm is hers again. Two of three.
Only the ruby remains, in the hands of a madman.
Next, the ruby.
The ruby calls to her across an ocean, like her own voice heard from another room.
The Fates said the ruby went to Ethel Cripps's son.
John Dee has spent forty years in a madhouse, dreaming of that stone.
Tonight he walks out, and takes his mother's ruby back.
He sits down in an all-night diner, and begins to play with the people inside.
Every hour he twists their dreams a little further, and the whole world's dreams go wrong with them.
Dee sees her coming. The ruby turns on her, and she is nearly unmade.
She crawls into the stone itself, wounded, to finish it there.
She slips through the dreams of the waitress and the trucker, unseen.
And she steps inside the ruby itself, where he cannot see her coming.
Dee feels her inside his stone. He laughs, and stands, and lifts it high.
He smashes the ruby. He thinks it will kill her.
It does not. Everything she ever poured into that stone comes home to her.
Three of three.
On the diner floor lies a small, broken old man.
He sleeps in his old cell, dreaming kindly, for the first time in forty years.
There is no John Dee any more. Not even a memory of him.
She leaves him on the diner floor, awake and sane, remembering everything.
Helm, sand and ruby. All three are hers again. She should feel whole. She feels nothing at all.
On a park bench, someone is feeding the pigeons, and waiting for her.
Her older sister, Death. She meets every living thing at the end, and she is the one sibling Aurie has always loved.
Aurie walks her sister's rounds: an old violinist, a young mother, a stranger on a bridge.
Everyone meets Death in the end. And everyone is met kindly.
Aurie goes home with something she did not have before.
Death shrugs, kisses her cheek, and goes about her work alone.
Helm, sand and ruby. The Queen of Dreams is whole again.
But the Dreaming remembers everything she did to get them.
Somewhere, an old man is still waking up, again and again.
And in Hell, a queen in the ice is waiting for a promise to be kept.
End of Part Two.
Destiny's garden lies at the edge of everything. Aurie walks it alone.
Every path in it is a choice someone once made. The paths behind her rearrange themselves as she passes.
Destiny is blind. He is chained to a book that holds everything that was, and everything that will be.
Destiny turns a page, and the garden becomes a hall.
The Endless. Older than the gods, each the shape of something every living thing must face.
Death, her elder sister.
Desire, beautiful and cruel, who smells of roses.
You have smelled those roses before, in a sleeping girl's dream.
Despair, Desire's twin, quiet and grey.
Delirium, the youngest, who was once Delight.
And one chair is empty. Destruction walked away three hundred years ago, and nobody speaks of it.
Desire knows exactly where to cut.
Ten thousand years ago, Aurie loved a mortal queen named Nada. Nada refused her, and Aurie sent her to Hell for it.
Aurie passed her in the ice, on the way to her helm.
Desire leans forward, smiling. It has been waiting for this.
The table goes quiet. Death squeezes her hand.
This time, she means to keep a promise.
Desire smiles, as if this were exactly what it wanted.
Hell, again.
Aurie leaves the table. Behind her, Desire laughs softly.
Death watches her go, and says nothing.
But the woman in the ice is still there. The question will not go away.
Death looks away. Despair begins, very quietly, to cry.
Desire smiles. It has learned exactly what it came to learn.
Pride is a door that locks from the inside.
The family scatters, each to their own realm.
Aurie goes home to prepare. She is going back into Hell, for Nada.
Aurie tells herself she does not care what Desire thinks. She is lying.
Aurie goes home certain she was right. Death does not call on her for a long time.
Destiny closes his book. He already knows how this ends.
End of Part Three.
Aurie returns to Hell to free Nada, as she told her family she would.
Desire's words would not leave her. Within a week she is standing at the gates of Hell anyway.
A letter arrives, sealed in black wax. Lucifer wishes to see her, and Lucifer does not ask twice.
The last time she came here, she walked past Nada in the ice.
But Hell is empty.
Every cell stands open. Every chain lies slack. The damned, and the demons, are gone.
Only Lucifer remains, alone on his throne, as if he has been waiting for her.
Lucifer takes the knife to his own wings. He does not ask twice.
He walks out into the waking world, a free man, and leaves her holding the key to Hell.
Every power in creation will want it.
Aurie cuts. The wings fall away into a storm of feathers.
Lucifer thanks her, which he has never done before, and walks out into the waking world.
Every power in creation will want that key.
By the time Aurie is home, every realm has heard: the Lady of Dreams holds the key to Hell.
Lucienne is afraid. Whoever holds that key decides what Hell becomes, and every power refused may become an enemy.
So Aurie does what the old laws allow. She invites them all as guests, under her roof, where no guest may harm another.
They come with gifts, and with threats.
Odin All-Father, with Thor and Loki, wanting somewhere to wait out the end of the world.
Azazel, a lord of Hell, who wants his home back. In a jar at his elbow, a captured soul.
It is Nada's soul. When the demons left Hell, Azazel took her with him.
The envoys of Faerie: Cluracan, and his sister Nuala, sent along as a gift.
And two angels, sent by the Creator, who ask for nothing, and only wait.
Before the night is over, Aurie must choose.
Remiel takes the key. Hell will become a place where suffering heals.
Azazel shrieks. The jar cracks, and Nada's soul spills free into Aurie's hands.
Odin takes the key, and Loki smiles far too widely.
Nada's soul Aurie must buy from Azazel herself. It costs her a dream she loved.
Azazel opens the jar. Nada is free.
Hell will be worse than it ever was. That is on Aurie now.
Cluracan bows extravagantly. Hell will become a wild and strange court.
Nada's soul Aurie takes from Azazel by force, and Faerie stands beside her.
Later, alone, Aurie opens her hand. The small light inside it grows, and becomes a woman.
Nada stands free for the first time in ten thousand years.
She was a queen. She loved Aurie, and refused her, because a mortal who loves one of the Endless brings ruin on her people.
Aurie condemned her to Hell for it.
Nada weeps, and forgives her.
She chooses to be born again, far away, into a brand new life.
And Aurie, for the first time in ten thousand years, feels lighter.
Nada strikes her across the face, and walks into the light alone.
Nada refuses every gift, and leaves without a word.
Hell has new masters.
Heaven's angels hold the keys. The damned may heal there now.
Odin's Hell waits for the end of the world. Loki is still smiling.
Azazel's Hell is crueler than it ever was.
Faerie's Hell is a strange, dancing place. Nobody is sure what it is for.
Somewhere in the waking world, a man with no wings plays piano in a bar, and thinks of her kindly.
Nada is gone, born again into a life of her own.
Nada is gone, and she did not forgive.
And Nuala of Faerie stays behind in the Dreaming, a gift to its court, with a favour still to be called.
End of Part Four.
With her helm, her sand and her ruby, Aurie begins to rebuild her realm.
The palace rises out of the sand. The gates of horn and ivory close again. Dreams that fled come creeping home.
Aurie walked her sister's rounds. Something of that walk has stayed with her.
Then one evening Lucienne comes to her with a letter, sealed with the sign of a book.
Only one member of her family seals his letters that way.
Lucienne bows. Behind her spectacles, she looks worried.
Aurie turns to leave. Paul McGuire is on his knees in the dust, beside the chair.
Fifty years he has loved Alex Burgess. He has never once begged anyone for anything.
Aurie opens her hand. Alex falls into the first real sleep he has had in seventy years.
Paul holds him, and weeps, and does not let go.
Aurie walks out into the dawn.
Behind her, Paul begins to sing, very softly, to keep Alex company in the waking.
Out on the street, the rain has not stopped. Johanna is waiting.
She has buried a lot of people. She has never hated anyone the way she hates Aurie now.
Johanna does not forgive her. But she hears it, and for a moment they stand in the rain together.
Johanna spits at her feet. Her curse follows Aurie out of London, and into everything.
The realm is mended. But some prayers arrived while Aurie was in the glass, and no one was there to hear them.
Lucienne has kept every one. Tonight she brings the oldest still unanswered.
It is from Calliope, the eldest of the nine Muses. Once, long ago, Aurie's lover.
In 1927 an old writer trapped her and kept her in his house. When he died, a young novelist bought her.
His name is Richard Madoc. For three years he has used her, and every book he writes is praised as genius.
Calliope prayed to the Three. The Three told her: Dream is free again. Call to her.
A tall house in London. At the top of the stairs, a door with the lock on the outside.
The lock turns to sand in Aurie's hand. The door swings open.
Calliope sits on the narrow bed, wrists bound, as she has sat for sixty years. She does not look up.
She knows who has come. She has known that voice for three thousand years.
Aurie touches the cords at her wrists. They pour away as sand.
Calliope stands, for the first time in sixty years, and does not thank her. She does not need to.
Then Aurie goes downstairs to find Richard Madoc.
Calliope stays bound on the bed while Aurie goes down the stairs.
She says nothing. She has had a great deal of practice at waiting.
Madoc is at his desk with a glass of whisky, his latest prize on the shelf behind him.
He sees a pale woman in black standing in a room he locked. He understands at once who she has come for.
Ideas pour into Richard Madoc, faster than he can catch them. He writes until the paper runs out.
Then he writes on the walls, with his own fingers, until they bleed.
Upstairs, the cords at Calliope's wrists pour away as sand. She walks out into the morning.
Days later, Calliope asks Aurie to let him go. Aurie does. Not one idea remains to him, ever again.
Upstairs, the cords at Calliope's wrists pour away as sand. She walks out into the morning.
Calliope wants only one thing: for him to say aloud what he did.
Madoc confesses to the world. Then Aurie leaves him to whatever the world decides.
Calliope looks at Aurie for a long moment. You have changed, she says.
Aurie takes every idea he ever had. Madoc sits at his desk and cannot remember what a story is.
Upstairs, the cords at Calliope's wrists pour away as sand. She walks out into the morning.
Calliope watches it done, and does not look away. But she does not thank Aurie, either.
Lucienne has a list of the dreams and nightmares that fled while Aurie was gone. Most have come home.
Not the Corinthian. Aurie made him herself: a nightmare in the shape of a man, with small mouths where his eyes should be.
For seventy years he has been loose in the waking world, killing, and taking eyes.
Then a young woman named Rose Walker begins to dream, and all the lost dreams start drifting toward her.
Rose is searching America for her little brother. The Corinthian is drawn to her like a moth.
He has come here to speak at a convention, which the guests call a cereal convention. Every guest is a killer.
He is their hero. And Aurie is standing at the back of the hall.
Aurie raises her hand. The Corinthian comes apart into sand, and is gone.
Only a small white skull is left on the carpet. Where its eyes should be, two tiny rows of teeth.
Then Aurie turns to the killers in their chairs, and makes every one of them see exactly what they are.
The Corinthian bows. His shape loosens into sand, and drifts away toward the Dreaming.
Lucienne will lock that sand away until Aurie is ready to shape him again.
Then Aurie turns to the killers in their chairs, and makes every one of them see exactly what they are.
The Corinthian smiles, puts his glasses back on, and walks out into the night.
Somewhere in the Dreaming, a door that should be shut swings quietly open.
Rose has found her brother. Tonight she sleeps in an old boarding house in Florida.
She dreams. And the walls between the dreams of everyone in the house come down.
Every dreamer falls into one shared dream, and the shared dream begins to swallow the Dreaming.
Lucienne's library is coming apart, page by page. Rose Walker is a vortex.
Once in a great many ages, a vortex is born. If she is not stopped, every dreaming mind will be torn apart.
Aurie finds her at the centre of it, small and terrified.
Aurie raises her hand. Rose does not run. She only closes her eyes.
And a voice behind them says: wait.
Aurie lowers her hand. Around them, the library tears, shelf by shelf.
And a voice behind them says: there is.
An old woman stands in the dream. She is eighty-five, in a pale blue dressing gown, and she is smiling.
Unity Kincaid. The girl who fell asleep in 1916, while Aurie was in the glass, and slept for seventy years.
Aurie spoke with her once, in her dream, when she was ten.
Long ago, in that dream, Aurie promised the girl she would not be forgotten. Unity remembers.
Unity takes Rose's hand. The light of the vortex flows out of the girl and into the old woman.
Unity smiles, and closes her eyes, and is gone. Death is waiting for her, kindly.
The walls of the dreams close again. Rose wakes in Florida, alive, with her brother asleep in the next room.
Rose will never forget that the lady from her dreams raised a hand to kill her.
Desire lives in a vast statue of itself, shaped like a heart. Aurie walks straight in.
Desire made the vortex happen. It hoped Aurie would kill a child of her own family, and be destroyed for it.
Desire is lounging on a velvet couch, and does not pretend to be surprised.
For one moment, Desire looks afraid. Then the smile returns, a little thinner than before.
Aurie leaves. Behind her, Desire laughs, and the laugh goes on a little too long.
There is one more appointment Aurie keeps. She has kept it every hundred years for six centuries.
Aurie and her sister Death sit in the corner of a smoky London tavern, watching the living.
A loud young man named Hob Gadling is telling his friends that dying is a mug's game. He doesn't intend to do it.
Death laughs. She grants it, for her sister's sake, to see what happens.
Aurie walks over to his table. Meet me here in a hundred years, she tells him, and tell me if you still think so.
Hob is waiting. He is rich now, and he still loves every day of it.
A young writer in the corner, Will Shaxberd, begs Aurie for the gift of telling stories. She makes him a bargain.
Hob has lost everything, his money, his wife, his son. He still does not want to die.
Hob is rich again, in a powdered wig. He has made his money from ships that carry slaves.
Hob goes red, and blusters, and does not forget it. He sells the ships before the next century comes.
Aurie says nothing. Hob laughs and pours the wine, and the ships keep sailing.
Five hundred years. Hob is waiting, in a good Victorian coat, and he has had a few drinks.
He has worked something out. He has decided to say it, whatever it costs him.
Aurie stands, and walks out into the London fog.
Behind her, Hob calls out: I'll be here in a hundred years. I'll wait for you.
Hob grins like a boy, and orders another round, and Aurie lets him.
The tavern is a pub now. Hob sits at the corner table with two pints, one of them untouched.
He did not know where she had been. He only knew she had never once been late.
A hundred years ago she walked out on him. He has bought her a drink anyway.
Hob raises his glass. To friends, he says. Aurie raises hers.
They drink. Hob talks, and Aurie listens, and the afternoon goes by.
